items.stem: Which term describes the following? A mental representation of a sensory experience, which can be used to think about things.
items.answer: mental image
items.markingKey: (a) mental image: a mental representation of a sensory experience, which can be used to think about things.
options: mental image
convergent thinking
problem solving
mental set

items.stem: What is thinking? Name its two building blocks.
items.answer: Higher mental process manipulating and analysing information; building blocks – mental images and concepts.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: Higher mental process manipulating and analysing information; building blocks – mental images and concepts.

items.stem: Give a reason for the following: Concepts make thinking efficient.
items.answer: They group similar objects and events so that we need not treat each one as new.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: They group similar objects and events so that we need not treat each one as new. (1 mark for the reason, 1 for linking it to the statement).

items.stem: The following statement about nature of thinking and its building blocks is incorrect. Rewrite it correctly and justify your correction: "Thinking deals only with objects that are physically present."
items.answer: Thinking uses mental images and concepts of objects not present.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the corrected statement (Thinking uses mental images and concepts of objects not present.); 1 mark for a supporting fact from the NCERT chapter.

items.stem: Read the case and answer. Before leaving home, Neha pictures the route to her friend's house in her mind and decides where to turn. Identify the building block of thought illustrated.
items.answer: Mental image.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: mental image.

items.stem: "An architect can plan a building before it is built." Examine this statement with reference to nature of thinking and its building blocks.
items.answer: The statement is valid. Thinking uses mental images to represent objects not physically present.
items.markingKey: 3 marks: 1 for accepting or qualifying the statement, 1 for the reason (thinking uses mental images to represent objects not physically present.), 1 for supporting evidence from the chapter.

items.stem:
Study the extract below and answer the questions.
"Concepts help us organise knowledge so that it can be retrieved quickly. Thinking is the base of all cognitive activities. Thinking is mostly goal-directed. Thinking involves manipulation and analysis of information received from the environment."
(i) Explain the term 'natural concept', which is related to the theme of the extract. (1)
(ii) Using the extract and your own knowledge, explain the following: Concepts make thinking efficient. (1)
(iii) A student concludes: "A prototype is the least typical member of a category." Use your knowledge of the chapter to evaluate this conclusion. (2)
items.answer: (i) A concept formed from everyday experience, whose features are not clearly defined. (ii) They group similar objects and events so that we need not treat each one as new. (iii) The conclusion is wrong: A prototype is the most typical example of a concept.
items.markingKey: 1+1+2 marks: (i) A concept formed from everyday experience, whose features are not clearly defined. (ii) They group similar objects and events so that we need not treat each one as new. (iii) The conclusion is wrong: A prototype is the most typical example of a concept.

items.stem: Distinguish between 'natural concept' and 'artificial concept'.
items.answer: Natural concept: a concept formed from everyday experience, whose features are not clearly defined. Artificial concept: a concept with clearly defined rules and features, such as a square.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: 1 mark for explaining 'natural concept' (a concept formed from everyday experience, whose features are not clearly defined.) and 1 mark for 'artificial concept' (a concept with clearly defined rules and features, such as a square.), with the contrast between them made clear.

items.answer: Incubation: the stage of creative thinking in which one stops working on the problem consciously while ideas develop. Illumination: the stage of creative thinking in which the solution suddenly appears, the 'aha' experience.

items.stem: Which one of the following statements about creative thinking is correct?
items.answer: Creative thinking involves both divergent and convergent thinking.

options: Illumination is the first stage of creative thinking.
Convergent thinking produces many possible answers.
Ideas should be criticised immediately during brainstorming.

items.stem: Describe the four stages of the creative thinking process.

items.stem: In the study of creative thinking, the term 'convergent thinking' refers to:
items.answer: Thinking that leads to one correct answer to a problem
items.markingKey: (a) 'convergent thinking' means thinking that leads to one correct answer to a problem.
options: Thinking that leads to one correct answer to a problem
The ability to produce many ideas for a task or problem
The ability to produce ideas that are rare or unusual
The tendency to think of objects only in terms of their usual functions, which hinders problem solving

items.stem: Distinguish between 'babbling' and 'holophrase'.
items.answer: Babbling: the stage of language development, around six months, in which infants produce repeated sound combinations such as 'ba-ba'. Holophrase: a single word used by a young child to express a whole thought.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: 1 mark for explaining 'babbling' (the stage of language development, around six months, in which infants produce repeated sound combinations such as 'ba-ba'.) and 1 mark for 'holophrase' (a single word used by a young child to express a whole thought.), with the contrast between them made clear.

items.stem:
Read the following extract on problem solving, reasoning and decision making and answer the questions that follow.
"Deductive reasoning goes from the general to the particular. Judgement and decision making are interrelated processes. Mental set and lack of motivation are obstacles to problem solving."
(i) Solving a new problem in the same way as earlier problems, even when a simpler method exists, shows: (1)
(ii) Explain the term 'decision making' as it relates to this theme. (1)
(iii) Explain the reason behind the following: A person may fail to solve a problem that needs a new method. (2)
items.answer: (i) mental set (ii) Choosing one option from among several alternatives. (iii) Mental set makes people stick to methods that worked before.
items.markingKey: 1+1+2 marks: (i) mental set (ii) Choosing one option from among several alternatives. (iii) Mental set makes people stick to methods that worked before.

items.stem:

items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) Both are true and R explains A: they group similar objects and events so that we need not treat each one as new.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.answer: Incubation – setting the problem aside while ideas develop

items.stem: Read the case and answer. Needing to tighten a screw and having no screwdriver, Arun does not think of using the coin in his pocket. Name the obstacle to problem solving shown here and explain it briefly.
items.answer: Functional fixedness: objects are seen only in terms of their usual function, which blocks problem solving.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: 1 mark for naming it (functional fixedness); 1 mark for the explanation (objects are seen only in terms of their usual function, which blocks problem solving).

items.answer: It stops people from taking risks and trying unusual ideas.
